title: POC scoping - Benchmark planning & harness integration
summary: Kickoff POC scoping focused on benchmark planning and integrating DataHarbor's load scripts with Redwood's harness. Agreed on success criteria (latency & throughput targets, fidelity checks), workload sizing (token distribution, request mix, concurrency), and timeline: 2-week bench, 1-week analysis. Action items assigned: Redwood provides harness repo, sample streaming/non-streaming clients, and benchmarking checklist; DataHarbor provides representative scripts, sample dataset, and test account access.
topics: Workload sizing: tokens per request, request mix, concurrency
Streaming vs non-streaming behaviour and metrics
Benchmark harness integration: repo, scripts, auth
Load testing approach: steady-state vs burst, ramping
Timeline and deliverables for the 2-week POC
action_items: Owner: Mark Ellis | Item: Share Redwood benchmark harness repo (README + sample clients for streaming and non-streaming) | Due: 2026-05-24
Owner: Priya Shah | Item: Prepare example config files for target RPS/concurrency and prefix cache settings | Due: 2026-05-25
Owner: Nina Park | Item: Provide representative request scripts and a 1k-sample test set plus token distribution histogram | Due: 2026-05-23
Owner: Rohit Varma | Item: Provision test VPC endpoint and service account for Redwood test runner (if using private) or provide API key for hosted tests | Due: 2026-05-24
Owner: Mark Ellis | Item: Schedule benchmark run windows and 2-hour sync for mid-POC results review | Due: 2026-05-28
next_steps: Redwood to send harness link + checklist and example streaming client
DataHarbor to upload sample scripts and test dataset to shared folder
Both teams to agree on exact p95/p99 latency targets and RPS profile by Monday
Kickoff benchmark run planned for 2026-05-26 with 48-hour steady-state window
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-05-21 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Mark Ellis (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (DataHarbor CTO), Nina Park (ML Eng), Rohit Varma (SRE), Sara Gomez (PM)

00:00 Mark Ellis: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Mark, AE on this account, and Priya is our SE who will drive the technical bench work. um, can we do quick intros from the DataHarbor side?
00:12 Liam O'Connor: Yeah hi, Liam here, CTO at DataHarbor. We're trying to get a POC to validate cost and latency at our 100k monthly active endpoint usage profile.
00:20 Nina Park: Nina, ML engineer, I'll own the test scripts and the model evaluation for fidelity.
00:24 Rohit Varma: Rohit, SRE, I'll handle infra and access.
00:27 Sara Gomez: Sara, PM, overseeing success criteria and timelines.
00:30 Priya Shah: Great, thanks. The goal today is to scope the benchmark plan and how we'll integrate your existing load scripts with our harness. we'll cover streaming vs non-streaming, what metrics to capture, and timeline.
00:41 Mark Ellis: Quick framing — most customers run two flavors in POC: streaming (for chat-like sessions) and non-streaming / request-response (for single-shot generation). they have different perf profiles.
00:52 Liam O'Connor: Our primary use-case is a conversational summarization feature inside the app — low-latency streaming is preferred for UX, but we want to see non-streaming numbers for batch jobs.
01:05 Priya Shah: Ok good. first thing — success criteria. what are you measuring? typical buckets: latency (p95/p99), throughput (RPS and tokens/sec), cost per 1k tokens, and quality (fidelity/regression vs baseline). any other?
01:20 Sara Gomez: Also determinism and error rate — we have SLA implications.
01:23 Mark Ellis: Great. can you give us target numbers or ranges? plz rough is fine.
01:29 Liam O'Connor: We're targeting p95 under 300ms for the streaming token delivery where front-end expects incremental tokens, and for non-streaming p99 under 800ms for typical 512-token requests. For throughput, our steady-state RPS target is 120 RPS with bursts to 400 for short windows.
01:48 Priya Shah: That's helpful. can you confirm average tokens per request and max sequence lengths?
01:52 Nina Park: Average payload is ~280 tokens, 95th at 600. We have both short prompts (50–100 tokens) and long context pulls ~1k tokens occasionally.
02:03 Priya Shah: OK that distribution matters for batching and KV cache. Redwood will run benchmarks across the observed token histogram. We'll also test cold vs warm KV cache — cold meaning new sessions, warm meaning cached prefixes.
02:16 Rohit Varma: For the POC we prefer hosted Redwood endpoints first; if results look good we'll test on a private deployment in our VPC. that may change auth flow.
02:26 Mark Ellis: Understood. we can run hosted runs with your API key or run our harness in your VPC with a service account. We'll need a test account and sample scripts to plug into the harness.
02:38 Priya Shah: About the harness — we have a standard repo with a runner that accepts pluggable clients: a streaming websocket client, an http non-streaming client, and a load generator shim. We'll share sample configs for concurrency, ramp, and steady-state windows.
02:51 Liam O'Connor: How invasive is instrumenting our scripts? we have custom pre- and post-processing around the requests.
02:58 Priya Shah: The shim is thin — you can either run your scripts and just call our client lib, or you can hand us a wrapper shell script. ideally we get a small adapter (python) that calls your existing function to produce prompt + metadata, then passes it to our runner.
03:15 Nina Park: We prefer to keep logic local. we'll supply a set of runner calls that emit the same timestamps and tags you expect.
03:21 Priya Shah: Perfect. we'll also want to capture token-level timing for streaming — like first-byte, subsequent chunk gaps, and final token latency. For non-streaming we capture request start/finish, server processing time, backend tokenization cost.
03:35 Mark Ellis: Metrics we'll produce: p50/p95/p99 latencies, tokens/sec, request error rate, model output similarity vs baseline (ROUGE/BLEU-ish or embedding distance), CPU/GPU utilization on the instance (if we run dedicated), and cost estimates.
03:49 Sara Gomez: For the quality checks, Nina will define a small eval set. how do you handle model versioning and rollbacks during a bench? we want repeatability.
03:58 Priya Shah: We pin model versions in the harness config and snapshot the config and seed. we recommend running 3 repeats for each scenario to smooth noise. We'll store artifacts and logs for reproducibility.
04:12 Rohit Varma: If we move to private, we'll need instructions for KMS/HSM key handling, SAML SSO overlays, and audit logs. can Redwood's harness write to our logging stack?
04:23 Mark Ellis: Yes, our private deployment integrates with customer KMS and can ship logs to a customer s3 or SIEM. For hosted we can provide audit logs on request but there are retention limits. we'll share the security doc.
04:35 Priya Shah: On load profile: recommend ramp of 10 minutes to steady-state, 48-hour steady-state window for meaningful tails, and a few burst windows (5–10 minutes) at target burst RPS to test autoscale and token queuing.
04:50 Liam O'Connor: 48 hours sounds long — can we do 24 hours?
04:53 Priya Shah: For p99 tails, 24 hours is ok as initial; 48 gives better stability. for the POC we'll run a 24–48 hour steady-state depending on cost and priorities.
05:03 Nina Park: Also ask: streaming vs non-streaming — streaming metrics are tricky because UX relies on time-to-first-token as well as sustained throughput.
05:12 Priya Shah: Yep agree. we'll instrument first-byte and 95th chunk gap. we'll include a small simulated browser client to measure perceived latency under network conditions.
05:23 Mark Ellis: Another consideration: batching and quantization settings. If DataHarbor wants to test quantized model variants, we should include at least one quantized config to show unit-cost differences and any quality delta.
05:36 Nina Park: We'll want cost/quality tradeoff numbers. can you surface quantization profiles?
05:40 Priya Shah: Yes — we'll include recommended quant profiles and note any known quality regressions. we'll also capture per-token cost.
05:47 Rohit Varma: On the bench harness practicalities: what's the auth pattern? do you need VPN access if we run private?
05:53 Mark Ellis: If private, we'll ask you to open a bastion or allow our runner IP ranges; we'll use mTLS or signed service tokens. We'll provide detailed steps in the repo.
06:03 Sara Gomez: Timeline — what's realistic?
06:07 Mark Ellis: If we get scripts and access by Monday (2026-05-24) we can prep configs and run an initial smoke within 48 hours, schedule full benchmark for 2026-05-26 start, run 24–48 hours, then a 1-week analysis window with a mid-POC sync.
06:22 Liam O'Connor: That timeline works for us. we'll target delivering scripts and test data by 2026-05-23 EOD.
06:29 Priya Shah: Great. ok let's drill into details on the scripts. Nina, can you describe typical request flow?
06:34 Nina Park: Sure. user triggers a summarization request with conversation history (up to 1k context), we do retrieval and add up to 3 docs, then call the model. We'll attach metadata for user-level routing and include a small set of tool calls we want the model to optionally call. The average output is 150 tokens.
06:51 Priya Shah: Do you need function/tool calling to be exercised in the bench?
06:55 Nina Park: Yes, about 20% of requests trigger a tool call — it's important because it changes latency and error modes.
07:02 Mark Ellis: We'll include a request mix config: 60% short chat (50–200 tokens), 30% mid (200–600), 10% long (600–1200), and enable tool calling for 20% of requests. We'll map that to the runner.
07:18 Rohit Varma: For load generator, can we reuse k6 or wrk?
07:22 Priya Shah: We currently have an adapter for k6 and a lightweight python runner. If you prefer wrk we can provide a shim. The key is that the generator tags requests with a session id so we can measure prefix cache hit rates.
07:35 Liam O'Connor: Ping on metrics export: we'll want Prometheus + Grafana dashboards and raw CSV logs for posthoc analysis.
07:42 Mark Ellis: We'll export Prom metrics and push logs to your S3; we'll also share a dashboard template.
07:48 Nina Park: A couple of gotchas — we saw sticky p99 increases when concurrency hit the GPU batch size limits. do you have guidance to interpret batching artifacts?
07:58 Priya Shah: Yes, we'll capture batch size distribution and sample latency vs batch size. that helps interpret p99 spikes. also KV cache hit vs miss ratios will be reported.
08:10 Sara Gomez: Anything around cost calc? how do you estimate production unit costs from bench?
08:15 Mark Ellis: We'll provide a cost model: tokens/sec * instance cost + amortized infra + storage. we'll produce an estimated $ per 1k tokens for each config (streaming vs non-streaming, quantized vs full).
08:27 Liam O'Connor: Ok good. Questions from our side — can the harness replay deterministic seeds so we can compare output deltas across runs?
08:34 Priya Shah: Yes, harness supports seed plus config snapshot. We'll save model outputs for each request id.
08:40 Mark Ellis: I'll recap next steps and action items. recap: Redwood shares harness repo and sample streaming client; DataHarbor shares scripts and dataset; agree on final targets Monday; run benchmark starting 2026-05-26; mid-POC sync during run; final analysis within one week of run.
08:58 Liam O'Connor: Sounds good. thanks everyone.
09:02 Mark Ellis: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the repo link and checklist.
09:06 End of meeting (approx 45m)

Notes: Transcript contains some filler and minor transcription errors. speaker turns occasionally overlap. References to KV cache, batching, quantization, streaming first-byte latency, and function/tool calling included. Links shared during call: [redwood-benchmark-harness-repo] (will be emailed), [security-ops.pdf] (redwood security doc)
